name: Pasteur Institute
scientists: Louis Pasteur; Émile Roux; Alexandre Yersin; Charles Nicolle; Luc Montagnier; Françoise Barré-Sinoussi
significance: Founded by Pasteur following the success of his rabies vaccine; became a leading center for microbiology and immunology, later the site of HIV's isolation in 1983.

name: Robert Koch's laboratory
scientists: Robert Koch; Friedrich Loeffler; Emil von Behring
significance: Where Koch developed his postulates and identified the tuberculosis and cholera bacilli, training a generation of bacteriologists who went on to found the field in their own countries.

name: Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory
scientists: Alfred Hershey; Martha Chase; Barbara McClintock
significance: Site of the Hershey-Chase blender experiment confirming DNA as genetic material; remains a leading center for genetics and molecular biology research.

name: Rockefeller Institute for Medical Research
scientists: Oswald Avery; Colin MacLeod; Maclyn McCarty
significance: Where Avery, MacLeod, and McCarty conducted the 1944 experiments identifying DNA as the carrier of genetic information.

name: Cavendish Laboratory
significance: Where Watson and Crick built their model of the DNA double helix in 1953, using X-ray diffraction data produced by Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins at King's College London.

name: Carl Woese's laboratory, University of Illinois
significance: Where 16S rRNA sequencing revealed Archaea as a domain of life distinct from Bacteria in 1977.

name: Selman Waksman's laboratory, Rutgers University
significance: Where streptomycin was isolated from Streptomyces griseus in 1943, the first effective treatment for tuberculosis.

name: Doudna Laboratory, University of California, Berkeley
scientists: Jennifer Doudna; Emmanuelle Charpentier (collaborating from Umeå, Sweden)
significance: Where research on bacterial CRISPR immune systems was developed into the CRISPR-Cas9 gene-editing tool, earning the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
